He also wants to eliminate all deductions, except charitable and mortgage deductions, which would raise the effective tax rate for a great many people.

He also has said that he's going to eliminate payroll taxes, but has sort of been wishy-washy as to whether or not he's going to replace them with a Value-Added Tax (V.A.T).

He says he's going to make up for the shortfall with massive, across the board spending cuts, raising the retirement age, means-testing social security, and a Balanced Budget Amendment to the Constitution.

The analysis is probably based in some way on a laffer curve. Basically, the relationship between tax rates and tax revenue isn't linear. Assuming you actually collect the taxes imposed, by raising rates you can begin to stifle growth. If you have more growth you have a bigger tax base, which can provide more revenue. You can see that the relationship isn't linear by looking at a graph of top marginal rates vs tax revenue collected over the last 80 years. The top rate has been over 90% at one point, but the amount of tax revenue collected has always remained between about 15.5%-18% of gdp. The reason is a lot of it is never collected because rich people can higher tax advisers and lobbyists to find a way around them, and people would rather stay home than work for 10 cents on the dollar, especially when they are rich already.

Take the example of a pizza. You're really hungry. Do you want 1/3 of a medium pizza, or 1/4 of a large pizza? Well you want the most pizza, but in order to find out which is deal gets you more food, you have to know how much larger the large pizza is that the medium pizza. 25% of the large could be substantially more pizza that 33.3% of the medium.
